name: Kola nut
what_people_do: Chew kola nut for alertness and stamina, offer it in hospitality and ritual, and (in one Nigerian custom) rub a kola paste on a pregnant belly.
why_they_say_it_works: It is a stimulant and a symbol of welcome; some say it stops hunger and fatigue.

documented_by.source: Erinfolami A et al 2011, Ment Illn, PMID 25478098
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Osogbo, Nigeria: 385 secondary school students; 30-day prevalence 11.2%, one-year 29.1%, lifetime 74.8%; most started at 14 or younger.

documented_by.source: Iweze FA 1983, J Nurse Midwifery, PMID 6552278 (Bendel State, Nigeria)
documented_by.quote_or_summary: Bendel State: kola paste rubbed on the abdomen in pregnancy to protect the newborn from thrush and skin infection.

evidence.tested: Associations with kola chewing in schoolchildren
evidence.finding: Use linked to lower age group, poor school attendance and family factors; authors urge awareness of dangers among adolescents.

source.name: Erinfolami A et al 2011, Ment Illn, PMID 25478098

evidence.finding: My search found only rat and agronomy papers on kola; no human trial.

source.name: agent4-traditional-practices.md, 12 Nov 2026 (research file in this project)

harm_note: Contains caffeine-type stimulants (general); linked here only to social and school correlates, not to a physical harm.
gaps: Entry now exists; caffeine content and heart effects not sourced.
